title: Atlas: Learning to Optimally Memorize the Context at Test Time
authors: Ali Behrouz, Zeman Li, Praneeth Kacham, Majid Daliri, Yuan Deng, Peilin Zhong, Meisam Razaviyayn, Vahab Mirrokni (Google)
tldr: Atlas is the third installment in the Google Titans/Miras line of test-time-memorization sequence models. It diagnoses three independent weaknesses in modern recurrent memory modules -- (1) online, one-token-at-a-time memory updates, (2) memory capacity bounded at O(d_k) stored associations for matrix memories, and (3) memory managed by plain first-order gradient descent -- and fixes each: the Omega rule replaces the per-token inner loss with a sliding-window loss over the last c tokens weighted by learned per-token gates; polynomial (degree-p) or infinite-dimensional exponential feature maps on keys lift capacity from O(d_k) to O(d_k^p) or unbounded; and the Muon optimizer (Newton-Schulz-orthogonalized momentum) replaces gradient descent inside the inner loop, giving an approximately second-order, 'locally optimal' memory update that remains chunkwise-parallelizable. The same machinery yields DeepTransformers and Dot, Transformer-like architectures that are strict generalizations of (unnormalized) softmax attention. At 1.3B params / 100B FineWeb tokens Atlas beats Transformer++, Titans, and Gated DeltaNet on language modeling and commonsense reasoning, and it holds >=80% accuracy at 10M-token context on BABILong where Titans degrades.
problem_and_motivation: The paper starts from the standard efficient-sequence-modeling tension: softmax attention is an exact, non-parametric associative memory whose KV cache grows with sequence length (quadratic time, linear-in-L memory at decode), while modern recurrent alternatives (RetNet, GLA, Mamba-2, DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet, RWKV-7, TTT, Titans) compress context into a fixed-size state. Despite strong average-quality results, these recurrent models still fail at long-context understanding, in-context retrieval, and length extrapolation. Atlas attributes this to three disjoint design defects. First, the ONLINE nature of the update: virtually every recurrent model optimizes its internal objective ('attentional bias' in the Miras vocabulary) only with respect to the current token (k_t, v_t) while retaining the previous state -- a greedy, token-by-token memorization that never asks whether the last c tokens are JOINTLY well-stored. In memory-metaphor terms, existing models measure the 'surprise' of a single token (Titans adds momentum, i.e., an exponentially decayed accumulation of past per-token surprises, but the loss itself is still per-token); an event spanning many tokens can be memorable without any individual token being surprising. Second, LIMITED MEMORY CAPACITY: the authors formalize capacity as the maximum number of linearly independent (key, value) pairs a memory can map exactly, and prove that the ubiquitous matrix memory with l2 regression loss stores only O(d_k) pairs -- sub-linear in its d_k*d_v parameters -- and that even deep MLP memories remain subquadratic. Third, WEAK MEMORY MANAGEMENT: the inner optimizer is almost always vanilla (online) gradient descent, a first-order method that can converge to poor local minima of the inner objective, i.e., learn low-quality key->value mappings; no prior parallelizable recurrent model exploits (approximate) second-order information. A terminological note the paper insists on: it prefers 'test-time memorization' over 'test-time training', because the inner loop only stores/retrieves information within the current context -- no persistent skill acquisition survives clearing the memory; the outer-loop (pre-trained) weights and initial states are untouched at inference.
core_mechanism:
=== 0. The Miras two-level template (inherited from 2504.13173) ===
Every model in the paper is specified by three choices: (a) a memory ARCHITECTURE M(.) with inner-loop parameters \theta_M (here: a 2-layer residual MLP, or a plain matrix as ablation); (b) an internal objective ('attentional bias') \ell(M; k, v) measuring how well M maps key k to value v; (c) an inner OPTIMIZER that turns the objective into a recurrent state-update rule. Keys/values/queries are outer-loop projections of the input x in R^{N x d_in}: K = xW_K, V = xW_V, Q = xW_Q.

=== 1. Capacity theory: why feature maps ===
Definition of capacity: the maximum number m of pairs (k_i, v_i) with linearly independent keys that M can map EXACTLY (zero inner loss).
Proposition 1 (matrix memory): For M in R^{d_v x d_k} with \ell(M; k_t, v_t) = ||M k_t - v_t||_2^2 optimized by GD, capacity is at most O(d_k). Proof: exact storage means MK = V with K = [k_1 ... k_m]; vectorizing gives (K^T \otimes I_{d_v}) vec(M) = vec(V), i.e., m d_v equations in d_k d_v unknowns, so m <= d_k. The bound is tight (M* = V K^T attains it via pseudoinverse when K has full column rank), and full-batch GD with step 0 < \eta < 2/\lambda_max(KK^T) converges to the minimum-norm interpolant (implicit bias of GD). So a d_k x d_v-parameter memory stores only d_k associations -- capacity is SUB-linear in parameter count. The same rank argument is the 'low-rank bottleneck' of multi-head attention.
Theorem 1 (deep memory): An MLP memory with L_M >= 2 layers, input dim d_k, hidden dims d_h^{(j)} stores at least O(d_k d_v) and at most O( d_k d_v \sum_{i=1}^{L_M} min_{j>=i} d_h^{(j)} d_h^{(i+1)} ) pairs. Proof sketch: with ReLU, the MLP is piecewise affine; on a fixed activation pattern M(.) = A(.)+B with A = W^{(L_M)} D^{(L_M-1)} W^{(L_M-1)} ... D^{(1)} W^{(1)} (D diagonal 0/1), and m <= rank(A), which is bounded by the min widths along the composition. Interpretation: depth strictly HELPS capacity (not just expressivity), but the bound stays subquadratic in (d_k, d_v) -- deep memory alone cannot give super-linear capacity.
Proposition 2 (polynomial features): Replace keys by \phi_p(k), where \phi_p(x) = [x^\beta]_{|\beta| <= p} is the vector of all monomials of degree <= p (dimension D = binom(d_k + p, p) = Theta(d_k^p) for fixed p). A matrix memory over lifted keys, \ell = ||M \phi_p(k_t) - v_t||_2^2, has capacity at most O(d_k^p), and no optimizer whatsoever can exceed D (rank argument on \Phi = [\phi_p(k_1) ... \phi_p(k_m)]). So a polynomial kernel on keys buys polynomially more capacity WITHOUT adding input-projection parameters.
Two further motivations for polynomial maps: (i) Softmax approximation -- exp(q_i^T k_j) ~ a_0 + a_1 q_i^T k_j + a_2 (q_i^T k_j)^2 + ... + a_p (q_i^T k_j)^p with LEARNABLE coefficients a_i initialized to 1/i! (Taylor series); the polynomial kernel is thus a truncated, learnable softmax kernel. (ii) Input feature gating -- the a_i act as gates over feature orders: a_i -> 0 prunes the order-i feature block, a_1 -> 1 with the rest 0 recovers \phi(x) = x; this is RNN-style gating applied to the INPUT representation rather than to the memory.
The infinite-dimensional limit: \phi^*(x) = (1, x, x^{\otimes 2}/\sqrt{2!}, x^{\otimes 3}/\sqrt{3!}, ...)^T (self-tensoring via Kronecker powers, following PolySketchFormer) satisfies exp(q^T k) = \phi^*(q)^T \phi^*(k) exactly, so the exponential kernel is a separable kernel into an infinite-dimensional space -- 'softmax attention as an associative memory has UNBOUNDED memory', which the paper offers as the root explanation of why attention out-memorizes fixed-state RNNs.

=== 2. The Omega rule: memorize the context, not the token ===
Standard online models solve min_M \ell(M; k_t, v_t) + Ret_t(M, M_{t-1}) (retention gate Ret keeps M near M_{t-1}). The fully global alternative min_M \sum_{i=1}^t \ell(M; k_i, v_i) (Mesa-layer style) is (i) inefficient -- it needs all past keys/values cached at test time and non-parallelizable exact solvers, and (ii) cannot prune stale/irrelevant context. Atlas's middle ground is a SLIDING-WINDOW inner objective. Omega rule: given window length c >= 1,
  min_M \sum_{i=t-c+1}^{t} \gamma_i^{(t)} || M(k_i) - v_i ||_2^2    (Eq. 9)
optimized by gradient descent (or any optimizer -- see Muon below). The \gamma_i^{(t)} in [0,1] are INPUT-DEPENDENT per-token gates acting as hard in-context pruning switches: \gamma -> 0 removes token i from the window's optimization entirely; \gamma -> 1 fully includes it. Only c gates are needed per step (constant), which is exactly why the sliding window makes learned gating affordable -- input-dependent gates over the FULL prefix (Eq. 7) would blow up parameters/memory. Limiting cases: c = 1 recovers the online Delta rule (and, with momentum, exactly Titans' LMM update M_t = \alpha_t M_{t-1} + S_t, S_t = \theta_t S_{t-1} - \eta_t \nabla \ell(M_{t-1}; k_t, v_t)); c = full context recovers global least-squares min_M \sum_{i=1}^t ||M k_i - v_i||_2^2, whose recursive Sherman-Morrison solution is the (non-parallelizable, linear-memory-only) Mesa-layer. Interpretation in the surprise metaphor: the gradient of the windowed loss is the 'surprise of the CONTEXT' -- a context-aware combination of the last c tokens -- rather than the surprise of one token.
OmegaNet = Omega rule + polynomial keys + GD + weight decay:
  M_t = \alpha_t M_{t-1} - \nabla \sum_{i=t-c+1}^{t} \gamma_i^{(t)} || M(\phi(k_i)) - v_i ||_2^2   (Eq. 10; gradient at M_{t-1}, per-token learning rates \eta_i^{(t)} absorbed into \gamma)
Linear-memory closed form (Eq. 11):
  M_t = ( diag(\alpha_t) - \sum_{i=t-c+1}^{t} \gamma_i^{(t)} \phi(k_i)\phi(k_i)^T ) M_{t-1} - \sum_{i=t-c+1}^{t} \gamma_i^{(t)} v_i \phi(k_i)^T
i.e., a rank-c generalization of the (gated) delta rule's rank-1 (I - \beta_t k_t k_t^T) transition. Symbols: \alpha_t in [0,1] is the input-dependent weight-decay/forget gate; \gamma_i^{(t)} the window gates; \phi the polynomial map; c the window.

=== 3. Atlas: Muon as the inner-loop optimizer ===
Even with Omega + feature maps, GD is first-order and can park the memory at poor local minima of the inner loss. Atlas optimizes the SAME windowed objective with Muon (Jordan et al. 2024) with weight decay:
  M_t = \alpha_t M_{t-1} - \eta_t NewtonSchulz-k(S_t)          (Eq. 32)
  S_t = \theta_t S_{t-1} + \nabla \sum_{i=t-c+1}^{t} \gamma_i^{(t)} || M(\phi^*(k_i)) - v_i ||_2^2   (Eq. 33; App. D.4 writes the momentum with a minus sign and per-token \eta_i^{(t)} -- S_t = \theta_t S_{t-1} - \sum \eta_i^{(t)} \nabla ||M_{t-1}(\phi(k_i)) - v_i||_2^2, M_t = \alpha_t M_{t-1} + NS5(S_t); the sign/step-size bookkeeping differs cosmetically across Table 1, Eq. 32-33, and App. D.4 but the algorithm is the same: decayed momentum over windowed gradients, then Newton-Schulz orthogonalization, then a gated decay step)
Symbols: S_t is the momentum state (same shape as each memory weight matrix); \theta_t the input-dependent momentum decay; \eta_t the learning-rate gate; NewtonSchulz-k(S) runs k iterations of the Newton-Schulz matrix iteration, which converges (k -> infinity) to the nearest semi-orthogonal matrix to S, i.e., UV^T from the SVD S = U\Sigma V^T. Why: replacing the raw momentum by its orthogonalization equalizes the singular values of the update -- Muon's rationale -- which the paper reads as approximating second-order information; hence Table 1 marks Atlas as the only parallelizable recurrent model that is 'locally optimal' (manages memory using approximate second-order information about tokens). The iteration count k is explicitly framed as an internal TEST-TIME-COMPUTE knob: more NS steps => better orthogonalization => potentially better memorization, at more inference FLOPs. In practice k = 5 ('NS-5' / 'Newton-schulz5').

=== 4. Transformer-like family: DLA, SWLA, DeepTransformers, Dot, SWDT ===
DLA (Deep Linear Attention, baseline): dot-product attentional bias \ell = <M(\phi(k_t)), v_t> with a DEEP MLP memory, GD + decay: M_t = \alpha_t M_{t-1} - \eta_t \nabla <M_{t-1}(\phi(k_t)), v_t>. With linear memory this collapses to gated linear attention W_t = \alpha_t W_{t-1} + v_t k_t^T -- so DLA isolates the value of deep memory in the Hebbian/linear-attention setting.
SWLA: same dot-product bias summed over the sliding window: M_t = \alpha_t M_{t-1} + \sum_{i=t-c+1}^t \gamma_i^{(t)} v_i \phi(k_i)^T (linear-memory closed form) -- a windowed, gated Hebbian rule.
Attention-as-regression connection: softmax attention is the NON-PARAMETRIC solution of a Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression M* = argmin_M \sum_{i=1}^L s(k_i, q) ||v_i - M||_2^2 = \sum_i s(k_i,q) v_i / \sum_j s(k_j,q); restricting the sum to the last c tokens gives exactly sliding-window attention (SWA). Reading: attention GLOBALLY optimizes its attentional bias non-parametrically, while modern RNNs are parametric ONLINE learners; the Omega rule imports attention's window-level optimization into the parametric world.
DeepTransformers: take DLA and replace \phi with the exact exponential feature map \phi^*: M_t = M_{t-1} - \nabla <M_{t-1}(\phi^*(k_t)), v_t>. With linear memory, M_t = \sum_{i<=t} v_i \phi^*(k_i)^T and y_t = M_t \phi^*(q_t) = \sum_{i<=t} v_i exp(q_t^T k_i) -- exactly UNNORMALIZED softmax attention. Hence DeepTransformers (deep memory + \phi^*) STRICTLY GENERALIZE Transformers: the Transformer is the special case (linear memory, Hebbian rule, exp kernel). SWDT is the sliding-window variant.
Dot (Deep Omega Transformer): replace the Hebbian rule with the Omega rule under \phi^*:
  M_t = M_{t-1} - \nabla \sum_{i=t-c+1}^t \gamma_i^{(t)} || M(\phi^*(k_i)) - v_i ||_2^2   (Eq. 27)
Linear-memory closed form: M_t = (I - \sum_{i=t-c+1}^t \gamma_i^{(t)} \phi^*(k_i)\phi^*(k_i)^T) M_{t-1} - \sum \gamma_i^{(t)} v_i \phi^*(k_i)^T, giving output y_t = M_t \phi^*(q_t) = (I - \sum_i \gamma_i^{(t)} \phi^*(k_i)\phi^*(k_i)^T) M_{t-1}\phi^*(q_t) - \sum_i \gamma_i^{(t)} v_i exp(q_t^T k_i). At c = 1 this is 'Transformers with Delta rule': unbounded memory that both APPENDS the new (k, v) like attention and SUBTRACTS the previously predicted value for that key -- an error-correcting attention. Both DeepTransformers and Dot are stated without the softmax normalizer (Table 1 footnote: 'without normalization').

=== 5. Backbone and memory architecture ===
Backbone follows modern recurrent LMs: per-layer linear projections for Q/K/V + short (size-4) depthwise convolutions + normalization on q, k for stability. Memory module: 2-layer residual MLP M(x) = x + W_1 \sigma(W_2 x) with GELU and expansion 4 (App. E adds layer norm at the end of each chunk). Atlas++ upgrades the memory to a GATED MLP: M(x) = x + W_1( \sigma(W_2 x) \otimes W_3 x ) (elementwise product; W_1, W_2, W_3 learnable in the INNER loop). Hybrids follow Titans: MAG (memory-as-gate, parallel branch gated with SWA output), MAL (memory-as-layer, memory block before an SWA block), and MAC (memory-as-context, used for BABILong, here WITHOUT persistent memory tokens). Design rationale summary per component: window loss (context vs token memorization) -> retrieval quality and long-context robustness; \gamma gates -> in-context pruning of irrelevant windows; \phi_p / \phi^* -> capacity O(d_k) -> O(d_k^p) -> unbounded; deep/gated MLP memory -> capacity multiplier and nonlinear key->value mappings; Muon/NS-5 -> escape first-order local minima ('locally optimal'); \alpha_t decay -> bounded state and forgetting; momentum \theta_t -> carries surprise across tokens (inherited from Titans).
outer_loop_training:
WHAT IS META-LEARNED (outer loop, standard backprop + AdamW): all projections W_Q, W_K, W_V, the size-4 conv layers, output blocks/MLPs, normalizations, AND the networks that emit the per-token inner-loop hyperparameters -- forget/decay gate \alpha_t, learning-rate gate \eta_t, momentum gate \theta_t, and the c window gates \gamma_i^{(t)} (all input-dependent, so they are small learned functions of x_t), plus the learnable polynomial coefficients a_i (initialized to 1/i!) of the feature map. Also the INITIAL memory parameters (the inner-loop MLP's initialization) are outer-loop state, per the Miras framing where everything except \theta_M = {W_1, W_2, ...} is outer-loop. Note for inference-only readers: 'the memory is trained at test time' does NOT mean the pre-trained checkpoint changes -- the outer loop learns, once, HOW the inner loop should update (via the gate networks and initial state), and the inner loop then re-runs from that initialization inside every context.
HOW GRADIENTS FLOW THROUGH THE INNER LOOP: the inner update rule (Eqs. 10/32-33) is itself a differentiable computation graph -- a sequence of gradient evaluations, gate multiplications, momentum accumulations, and Newton-Schulz matrix polynomials. Outer-loop backprop differentiates through this whole unrolled recurrence, so the outer gradient for, e.g., W_K includes terms through \nabla_M ||M(\phi(k_i)) - v_i||^2 (a second-derivative-style term, as in TTT/Titans). The paper does not dwell on this (it inherits the machinery from Titans), but it is why the chunkwise formulation below matters: it is the graph actually differentiated.
CHUNKWISE-PARALLEL FORMULATION (Sec. 3.3, the trick that makes training feasible): a naive Omega implementation materializes c gradient matrices \nabla\ell in R^{d_in x d_in} per position -- prohibitive memory/IO. Instead, split the length-L sequence into chunks S_i of size b; within a chunk compute ALL per-token gradients with respect to the FROZEN state at the chunk boundary, M_{t'} with t' = t - mod(t, b) (this is the same intra-chunk linearization used by Titans and TTT: exactness is traded for parallelism -- inside a chunk the memory used in the gradient is b steps stale at worst). With \gamma_i^{(t)} = \eta_t for exposition, the exact b=1 recurrence M_t = \alpha_t M_{t-1} - \eta_t \sum_{i=t-c+1}^t \nabla\ell(M_{t-1}; k_i, v_i) becomes, inside a chunk (t' <= t < t'+b):
  M_t = (\alpha_t ... \alpha_{t'}) M_{t'} - \sum_{n=t'}^{t} (\alpha_t ... \alpha_{n+1}) \eta_n \sum_{i=n-c+1}^{n} \nabla\ell(M_{t'}; k_i, v_i)  =: (\prod \alpha) M_{t'} - G_t.
G_t is computed exactly as in Titans' parallel gradient computation, PLUS a sliding-window mask M_s applied during the einsum broadcast: M_s is the identity for c = 1, and for c > 1 it additionally sets to 1 the c-1 positions immediately preceding each diagonal entry -- i.e., a banded lower-triangular 0/1 matrix that sums gradient contributions over each position's window WITHOUT materializing per-position gradient tensors. So the window costs one extra banded mask in an existing matmul, and the authors claim no significant overhead versus the online (c=1) version.
MUON PARALLELIZATION (Sec. 5.1): the key observation is that, once gradients are taken at the chunk-boundary state (u_t := \nabla\ell(M_{t'}; k_t, v_t) precomputable for the whole chunk), the momentum recurrence S_t = \theta_t S_{t-1} - \eta_t u_t is INDEPENDENT of the evolving memory M. Unrolling: S_t = \beta_t S_0 - \sum_{i=1}^t (\beta_t / \beta_i) \eta_i u_i with \beta_t = \theta_t ... \theta_1 -- a linear scan expressible as broadcast-and-matmul (S = \beta S_0 - \Theta \odot E \odot G in their notation, with \Theta, E diagonal matrices of the \theta and \eta gates and G the stacked gradients). All S_t in a chunk are therefore computed in parallel, and Newton-Schulz-5 is then applied to every S_t simultaneously (it is a per-matrix polynomial: 5 iterations of X <- aX + b(XX^T)X + c(XX^T)^2 X -- pure batched matmuls, ideal for TPUs/GPUs): S'_t = NS5(S_t), M_t = \alpha_t M_{t-1} + S'_t (final step is a simple gated cumulative sum/scan). This makes Atlas, per the authors, the first PARALLELIZABLE recurrent architecture with an (approximately) second-order inner optimizer.
TRAINING RECIPE: FineWeb, T5 tokenizer (32K vocab), training context 4K (2K for SWA components), AdamW lr 4e-4 (peak LRs per scale: 3e-3 / 1.5e-3 / 1.25e-3 / 7e-4 for 170M/340M/760M/1.3B), cosine schedule, batch 0.5M tokens, weight decay 0.1. Scales: 170M/340M (15B tokens), 760M (30B), 1.3B (100B); blocks 12/24/24/18, dims 768/1024/1536/2048, heads 16/16/16/8.
inner_loop_test_time:
STATE THAT CHANGES DURING INFERENCE (per layer, per head): (1) the inner memory parameters \theta_M -- for the default memory, the weights of the 2-layer residual MLP M(x) = x + W_1\sigma(W_2 x) with expansion 4 (Atlas++: W_1, W_2, W_3 of the gated MLP); for the linear-memory ablation, a single matrix; (2) the Muon momentum buffer S_t, one tensor per inner weight matrix (same shapes as \theta_M); (3) a rolling buffer of the last c-1 keys/values (and their gates) needed to evaluate the windowed loss -- constant size, O(c(d_k + d_v)), NOT growing with sequence length. Nothing else changes: all outer-loop weights are frozen.
UPDATE RULE PER TOKEN (Atlas): compute k_t, v_t, q_t and gates (\alpha_t, \eta_t, \theta_t, \gamma^{(t)}) from frozen projections; form the windowed loss L_t(M) = \sum_{i=t-c+1}^t \gamma_i^{(t)} ||M(\phi(k_i)) - v_i||_2^2 over the current window buffer; take its gradient with respect to \theta_M; momentum update S_t = \theta_t S_{t-1} - (windowed gradient, gate-scaled); orthogonalize via 5 Newton-Schulz iterations; decay-and-step M_t = \alpha_t M_{t-1} + \eta_t-scaled NS5(S_t). Read out y_t = M_t(\phi(q_t)) (for the Transformer-like variants, y_t = M_t \phi^*(q_t), which the closed forms show equals unnormalized attention-style sums). OmegaNet is the same minus momentum/NS (plain GD). In deployment one would run this chunkwise exactly as in training (gradients at chunk-boundary state), which also batches the NS-5 matmuls; b and c are independent knobs.
PER-TOKEN COMPUTE: O(1) in sequence length -- the defining recurrent property. Concretely, per token per layer: one forward+backward through the 2-layer memory MLP for each of the c window terms IF computed naively, but the sliding-window mask reuses each token's gradient across the c windows it belongs to, so amortized cost is ~1 gradient evaluation per token plus the window-sum (a banded matmul); plus the NS-5 orthogonalization, ~5 iterations x ~3-4 matmuls each over matrices shaped like W_1, W_2 (e.g., d x 4d) -- this is the main constant-factor overhead over Titans, and it is pure matmul. The Newton-Schulz iteration count k is an explicit test-time-compute dial: larger k -> closer to exact semi-orthogonalization (SVD's UV^T) -> claimed better memorization, linearly more FLOPs. The polynomial map \phi_p multiplies key dimensionality (degree-2 self-tensoring takes d_k -> ~d_k^2 features before any sketching), inflating the memory MLP's first-layer width -- the capacity gain is paid for in state size and matmul width, not in cache growth.
MEMORY FOOTPRINT: fixed-size, sequence-length-independent: |\theta_M| + |S| + c-window buffer, versus a Transformer KV cache of 2 L_ctx d per layer. At the 10M-token BABILong setting this is the entire point: attention's cache is ~10^7 x d entries/layer while Atlas carries a few (expanded) d x 4d matrices.
The paper's own terminology stresses this is memorization, not training: clearing the state between contexts erases everything learned in-context; the checkpoint never changes.

concepts_introduced.name: Omega rule
concepts_introduced.definition: Sliding-window inner-loop update: optimize min_M sum_{i=t-c+1}^t gamma_i^{(t)} ||M(k_i) - v_i||_2^2 instead of a per-token loss; strictly generalizes the Delta rule (c=1) and interpolates to global least-squares (c=L). The gradient of the windowed loss is the 'surprise of the context'.

concepts_introduced.name: gamma window gates (in-context pruning)
concepts_introduced.definition: Input-dependent hard gates gamma_i^{(t)} in [0,1], one per token in the local window, that include/exclude individual tokens from the inner optimization; affordable only because the window makes the gate count constant (c per step).

concepts_introduced.name: OmegaNet
concepts_introduced.definition: Sequence model = deep MLP memory + Omega rule attentional bias + polynomial key/query features + inner gradient descent with weight-decay gate alpha_t.

concepts_introduced.name: Atlas
concepts_introduced.definition: OmegaNet's objective optimized with Muon in the inner loop: momentum over windowed gradients, Newton-Schulz-k orthogonalization, gated decay; the first parallelizable recurrent model with an approximately second-order ('locally optimal') memory update.

concepts_introduced.name: Atlas++
concepts_introduced.definition: Atlas with a gated-MLP memory M(x) = x + W_1(sigma(W_2 x) (x) W_3 x).

concepts_introduced.name: Memory capacity (formal)
concepts_introduced.definition: Maximum number of (key, value) pairs with linearly independent keys that a memory can map exactly. Matrix memory + l2 loss: O(d_k) (Prop 1); deep MLP: between O(d_k d_v) and a subquadratic width-dependent bound (Thm 1); degree-p polynomial features: O(d_k^p) (Prop 2).

concepts_introduced.name: Polynomial feature map phi_p with learnable Taylor gates
concepts_introduced.definition: phi_p(x) = all monomials of degree <= p; paired with learnable coefficients a_i (init 1/i!) it is a truncated learnable softmax-kernel approximation, and the a_i act as input-feature gates (imported from PolySketchFormer / dense associative memories, repurposed as a capacity mechanism for recurrent memory).

concepts_introduced.name: phi* (infinite-dimensional exponential feature map)
concepts_introduced.definition: phi*(x) = (1, x, x^{(x)2}/sqrt(2!), ...) via Kronecker self-tensoring; exp(q^T k) = phi*(q)^T phi*(k), framing softmax attention as an associative memory with unbounded capacity.

concepts_introduced.name: DeepTransformers
concepts_introduced.definition: Hebbian rule + phi* + deep memory; with linear memory reduces exactly to unnormalized softmax attention, hence a strict generalization of the Transformer.

concepts_introduced.name: Dot (Deep Omega Transformer)
concepts_introduced.definition: Omega rule + phi* + deep memory; at c=1 it is 'Transformers with Delta rule' -- attention that also error-corrects previously stored values for a key. SWDT is the sliding-window DeepTransformer.

concepts_introduced.name: DLA / SWLA
concepts_introduced.definition: Deep (gated) Linear Attention: dot-product bias with a deep MLP memory (linear-memory case = gated linear attention); SWLA is its sliding-window version. Introduced as controlled baselines isolating deep memory and windowed objectives.

concepts_introduced.name: Locally optimal memory
concepts_introduced.definition: Table-1 property: memory managed using (approximate) second-order information about tokens; attention/SWA have it non-parametrically, Atlas achieves it parametrically via Muon; all GD-based RNNs lack it.

concepts_introduced.name: Flexible context
concepts_introduced.definition: Table-1 property: ability to flexibly choose what part of the context to memorize (window + learned gamma gates); held by SWA, SWDT, OmegaNet, Dot, Atlas.

concepts_introduced.name: Test-time memorization (vs test-time training)
concepts_introduced.definition: Authors' preferred term: the inner loop stores/retrieves within the current context only; no persistent learning survives memory reset, and outer-loop weights never change at inference.

concepts_introduced.name: Newton-Schulz steps as test-time compute
concepts_introduced.definition: The NS iteration count k in NewtonSchulz-k(S_t) is an inference-time dial trading FLOPs for memorization quality (k -> infinity gives the nearest semi-orthogonal matrix to the momentum).

concepts_introduced.name: Sliding-window mask M_s
concepts_introduced.definition: Banded 0/1 mask (identity + c-1 sub-diagonal bands) applied during the chunkwise einsum so window-summed gradients are computed without materializing c gradient matrices per position.

assumptions_and_scope: Scope: decoder-style language models up to 1.3B params / 100B tokens, 4K training context; evaluation up to 10M tokens (BABILong, fine-tuned per the benchmark protocol). Claims are strongest for long-context memorization/recall; the paper does not evaluate state-tracking/formal expressivity (a distinct axis where delta-rule products, RWKV-7 etc. compete), reasoning, or downstream SFT/RLHF behavior. Key assumptions and caveats: (1) The capacity theory is about EXACT interpolation of linearly independent keys under piecewise-affine reasoning (single activation region for the MLP result) -- a clean but idealized proxy for practical retrieval quality. (2) The chunkwise training/inference form computes inner gradients at the stale chunk-boundary state M_{t'} (same approximation as Titans/TTT); the paper offers no bound on the gap versus the exact per-token recurrence. (3) Eq. 33 vs Table 1 vs App. D.4 differ in momentum sign and in where the learning-rate gate sits (eta_t outside NS in Eq. 32, per-token eta_i inside the sum with M_t = alpha M + NS5(S) in D.4) -- a re-implementer must pick one convention; the semantics (decayed momentum of windowed gradients, orthogonalize, gated decay step) are unambiguous. (4) DeepTransformers/Dot are analyzed UNNORMALIZED; the softmax denominator is dropped, and how normalization is restored in the trained models is not specified. (5) How phi* is realized with a DEEP memory is not spelled out -- the exact exp-kernel equivalence holds only for the linear-memory closed forms; with deep memory the infinite-dimensional feature vector cannot be materialized, so practical models presumably use truncated/polynomial features (the ablation 'w/o Polynomial Mapping' suggests phi_p is what is actually implemented in Atlas). (6) Degree-p features inflate key dimensionality ~d_k^p; the paper cites PolySketchFormer for sketching but never states the implemented p, sketch, or resulting dimensions. (7) Baseline numbers are largely inherited from Titans/Miras/Gated-DeltaNet papers rather than re-run. BACKGROUND SCAFFOLDING needed for inference-only readers: inner/outer loops and meta-learning ('backprop through an optimizer'); gradient descent, momentum, and weight decay as recurrence-defining objects rather than training tools; the Muon optimizer and Newton-Schulz orthogonalization (and why orthogonalized updates approximate second-order preconditioning); kernel feature maps / separability (phi(q)^T phi(k)) as the bridge between attention and RNNs; implicit bias of GD (min-norm solutions) used in Prop 1; the Miras vocabulary (attentional bias, retention gate) from 2504.13173.
experiments_and_scale: Scales: 170M/340M (15B FineWeb tokens), 760M (30B), 1.3B (100B); T5 tokenizer, 4K training context. Language modeling + commonsense (Wiki ppl, LAMBADA ppl/acc, PIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-e/c, SIQA, BoolQ): at 1.3B, Atlas reaches Wiki 14.97 / LMB 10.98 ppl, avg acc 57.62; Atlas++ 14.40/10.72, avg 58.03 -- vs Titans (LMM) 15.60/11.41, 56.82; Gated DeltaNet 16.42/12.17, 55.32; Transformer++ 18.53/18.32, 52.25; Samba 16.13/13.29, 54.00. The Transformer generalizations also win their comparison: DeepTransformers 56.19 and Dot 57.35 avg vs Transformer++ 52.25 (1.3B); same ordering at 760M (OmegaNet 52.56, Atlas 52.77, Atlas++/gated-mem 53.09, Titans 51.56, Transformer++ 48.69) and 340M. Hybrids: Atlas(MAG) 18.62 Wiki ppl / 53.08 avg at 760M, MAG > MAL. RULER S-NIAH (needle-in-haystack, 2K-16K on 4K-trained models): pure Atlas beats recurrent baselines (e.g., S-NIAH-N 16K: Atlas 84.0 vs Titans 80.2, DeltaNet 5.4, TTT 4.4); hybrids and the Transformer-like models are stronger still (Dot 96.8-100 across settings; Atlas MAG up to 98.6 at PK-16K), i.e., ~4x length extrapolation beyond training context. BABILong (MAC backbone without persistent tokens, fine-tuned): Atlas matches Titans to 1M tokens and holds >=80% accuracy at 10M where Titans drops -- the headline long-context claim. MAD synthetic suite: Atlas best average 79.50 (vs Transformers 75.46, Titans 76.44, Gated DeltaNet 71.04), with the largest margins in memorization (91.4) and fuzzy recall. In-context recall suite (SWDE/NQ/DROP/FDA/SQuAD/TQA): Transformers still lead overall (53.55 avg) but Atlas 43.70 and OmegaNet 43.13 close the gap over Titans 42.31 and Gated DeltaNet 40.28 -- an honest negative result: parametric fixed-size memory still trails attention on retrieval-heavy tasks. MQAR: best accuracy-per-memory-size vs DeltaNet-class baselines. Ablations (760M, Table 6): full Atlas 19.97 ppl / 52.77 acc; linear memory degrades to 21.03/49.74; c=1 (no Omega window) 21.98/49.26; no polynomial mapping 22.14/50.57; no Muon 19.65/52.56 (NOTE: removing Muon slightly IMPROVES perplexity while hurting reasoning accuracy -- Muon's benefit is task-dependent, the window and feature map carry more of the gain); gated-MLP memory helps (19.53/53.09). Fig. 5: performance improves monotonically with window c at fixed global context (the gamma gates prune when needed); Fig. 8: favorable scaling in both parameters and training context vs baselines. Learnability micro-study (Sec 6.4, d=256 online regression with Adam/RMSprop/SGD): online MLPs learn low-rank/MLP/attention-output mappings well but struggle when the target requires memorizing past inputs (attention+MLP, SWA+MLP settings), and notably do WORSE on sliding-window-attention targets than full-attention ones -- evidence that plain online learners fail to 'forget', motivating gated windowed objectives. No wall-clock throughput or kernel benchmarks are reported anywhere.
systems_implications: (1) State vs KV cache: Atlas's per-layer state is the inner MLP weights + Muon momentum + a c-token window buffer -- fixed size, O(1) in context. With d = 2048 (1.3B config), a 2-layer expansion-4 memory over raw keys is ~2 x (d x 4d) ~ 33.5M params/layer-head-group plus an equal-size momentum buffer; polynomial features multiply the first-layer input width (deg-2 ~ d_k^2 pre-sketch), so the ACTUAL state size hinges on the undisclosed feature dimension -- a first-order question for any serving-cost model. Against a Transformer KV cache (2 x L x d per layer), Atlas wins asymptotically and specifically at BABILong-scale contexts (10M tokens), but at short contexts its state+momentum can exceed a small KV cache: the crossover analysis is absent from the paper. (2) Compute character: everything in the inner loop is dense matmul -- windowed gradients via a banded einsum mask, momentum via broadcast scans, NS-5 via 5 matrix-polynomial iterations -- deliberately TPU/GPU-friendly ('tensorize computations and maximize matmuls'). NS-5 adds a constant-factor overhead over Titans (~15-20 extra square matmuls per update per weight matrix), batchable across positions in a chunk. (3) Parallelization: chunkwise (intra-chunk parallel, inter-chunk sequential scan), with the crucial structural fact that the momentum recurrence decouples from the memory state once gradients are taken at chunk boundaries -- so gradients, momenta, and NS-5 are all embarrassingly parallel within a chunk, and only the final alpha-gated accumulation is a scan. Sequence-parallel/context-parallel training maps on naturally. The sliding-window mask means Omega (any c) costs essentially the same as c=1: window length is nearly free at training time. (4) Test-time-compute dial: NS iteration count k trades decode FLOPs for memorization quality with zero state-size change -- an unusual serving knob (comparable to speculative-decoding-style quality/latency trades but inside the layer). (5) Decode latency: per-token work is constant but heavier than DeltaNet/Titans (deep-memory fwd+bwd, window sum, NS-5); the paper reports NO throughput/latency numbers, so the quality-per-FLOP story at serving time is unquantified. (6) Hybrids: MAG/MAL attach SWA (2K window) branches -- serving needs both a small rolling KV cache and the recurrent state; the pure-recurrent variant already beats some hybrids at LM quality, but the recall suite says attention still pays for retrieval. (7) Kernel engineering surface: fusing per-position NS-5 across a chunk, the banded gradient mask, and backprop-through-NS in the outer loop are the main new kernel workloads relative to Titans; none are open-sourced here. (8) The Transformer-like variants (DeepTransformers/Dot) with deep memory have attention-like cost profiles (phi* means no finite recurrent state in the exact case), so they compete on quality-vs-Transformer rather than on serving efficiency.
connections: LINEAGE BACKWARD, within this study set: Titans (2501.00663) supplies the deep neural memory, momentum-as-past-surprise, forget gate alpha_t, chunkwise gradient-at-boundary training, and the MAC/MAG/MAL hybrids; Atlas keeps all of it and changes the OBJECTIVE (per-token -> windowed Omega) and the OPTIMIZER (GD+momentum -> Muon). Titans is recovered exactly as Omega with c=1 + momentum. Miras / 'It's All Connected' (2504.13173) supplies the entire conceptual frame -- associative memory, attentional bias, retention gate, inner/outer loops -- plus the sibling models Moneta/Yaad/Memora used as baselines; Atlas extends Miras along the axis 'which tokens does the inner loss see' (window) and 'which optimizer' (Muon), and Table 1 is essentially the Miras taxonomy extended with two new columns (locally optimal, flexible context). EXTERNAL lineage: linear attention (Katharopoulos et al.) = Hebbian rule + linear memory; fast weight programmers (Schmidhuber 1992/93; Schlag et al.) = the key/value writable-memory idea; DeltaNet and parallel delta (Yang et al.) = the c=1, l2, GD special case, whose rank-1 (I - beta k k^T) transition Omega generalizes to rank-c; Gated DeltaNet and RWKV-7 = gated delta variants that Atlas beats at 1.3B; Longhorn = implicit (closed-form) online update, contrasted as still online; Mamba-2 as the SSM baseline; TTT (Sun et al. 2024) = deep memory + online GD, i.e., Omega with c=1 and no gates; Mesa-layer (Von Oswald et al.) = the c=infinity extreme solved exactly by Sherman-Morrison, which Atlas positions as non-parallelizable and unprunable; sliding-window attention = the NON-parametric solution of the same windowed regression Atlas solves parametrically (via Nadaraya-Watson); PolySketchFormer (Kacham et al., co-authors here) = the polynomial/self-tensoring feature machinery; dense associative memories / modern Hopfield (Krotov & Hopfield, Ramsauer et al.) = higher-order features raise capacity; Muon (Jordan et al.) imported from the outer-loop optimizer literature into the inner loop -- an instance of the broader pattern (run through this whole paper line) of transplanting optimizer research into architecture design. FORWARD, for the later papers in the set (2511.07343, 2512.24695, 2606.03979): Atlas establishes three reusable moves they can build on or contest -- window-level inner objectives, optimizer-as-architecture (momentum/Muon inside the layer), and capacity accounting via feature maps; its 'test-time memorization vs training' terminology and the k-steps-as-test-time-compute framing also recur in the nested-learning/self-modifying follow-ups. WHAT IT LEAVES OPEN explicitly/implicitly: attention still wins in-context recall (Table 5) -- fixed-size parametric memory has not closed the retrieval gap; Muon's perplexity benefit is equivocal in the ablation; normalization for DeepTransformers/Dot is dropped; no throughput data; no state-tracking/expressivity analysis; the exact-vs-chunkwise approximation is unquantified.
open_questions: (1) Retrieval gap: Atlas narrows but does not close the in-context-recall gap to Transformers (43.7 vs 53.6 avg) -- is this a capacity limit, an optimization limit, or fundamental to lossy fixed-state memory? (2) Muon's real contribution: the ablation shows removing Muon IMPROVES Wiki perplexity (19.65 vs 19.97) while hurting reasoning accuracy; when and why does second-order inner optimization pay, and does the NS-k test-time-compute knob actually yield a monotone quality curve (never measured)? (3) What is actually implemented for the feature map: degree p, sketching (PolySketchFormer-style?), and the resulting memory input dimension are unstated, yet they determine state size and FLOPs; likewise how phi* coexists with a deep memory outside the linear closed form. (4) No wall-clock numbers: training overhead vs Titans/GDN and decode throughput vs FlashAttention-served Transformers are unmeasured; the serving crossover (context length where fixed state beats KV cache in latency AND quality) is open. (5) Chunkwise staleness: gradients are taken at chunk-boundary states -- no analysis of the error vs the exact recurrence, or of the interaction between chunk size b and window c. (6) Window selection: c is a hyperparameter; Fig. 5 says bigger is better (gates prune), but cost, optimal schedules, or learned/adaptive c are unexplored. (7) Normalization: DeepTransformers/Dot are unnormalized generalizations of attention -- how much of softmax's stability/quality comes from the dropped denominator? (8) Sign/step-size discrepancies between Eq. 32-33, Table 1, and App. D.4 leave the canonical Atlas recurrence to be pinned down by an implementation. (9) The learnability study suggests online learners 'cannot forget' inside sliding windows -- whether Omega's gamma gates fully solve this at scale is asserted via benchmarks, not isolated. (10) Beyond 1.3B: does the advantage persist at modern production scales, under SFT/RL, and on state-tracking tasks where delta-rule expressivity results (DeltaProduct, RWKV-7) apply?
